title: Approximately efficient voluntary provision of global public goods

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a mechanism through which sovereigns or other uncompelled parties would voluntarily finance and provide a global public good at a quantity close to an explicitly defined efficient benchmark. Its central difficulty is that a party can decline participation and payment while still receiving benefits produced by others. The mechanism must make participation worthwhile relative to that benefit-retaining outside option, give parties appropriate incentives to reveal private information or take the required actions, and finance provision under a stated budget-balance rule.

As a synthesis of the proposed target, approximate efficiency means achieving a substantively large, declared share of the efficient outcome rather than requiring exact efficiency in every circumstance. The target combines incentive compatibility, voluntary participation, approximate efficiency and budget balance without relying on a world tax authority. A complete specification would identify the good, eligible participants, information available to each party, payment and provision rules, and the behavior expected when some parties refuse to join. This capability is hypothetical; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate its achievement.

significance.text: The revolutionary capability would be to finance substantial international cooperation while preserving the right to refuse payment and retain spillover benefits. Taxing authority changes this problem materially: a government can impose costs on people who do not participate, whereas the proposed mechanism must sustain participation without that power over sovereign parties. Success would expand the feasible set of global policy by making some provision achievable through incentives and voluntary financing.

The direct consequence of successful implementation would be funded provision of the demonstrated good at the tested scale, with participation, payments and output explained by the mechanism. Possible applications include climate stability, pandemic surveillance, antimicrobial restraint and the production or dissemination of basic knowledge. These are proposed applications, not interchangeable instances of a fully established model: each requires separate analysis of which benefits cross borders, what can be withheld, who bears costs, and what actions can be verified.

Broader consequences would remain conditional. One successful application would not establish durable international adoption, transfer to other goods or a universal escape from free riding. Nor would it settle how gains and burdens should be distributed. An efficient benchmark depends on valuations and modeling choices; particular welfare claims, including those involving a social cost of carbon, retain empirical and ethical uncertainty. The innovation would improve the ability to implement cooperation under specified conditions, while leaving those valuation questions to separate analysis.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a workable mechanism that jointly satisfies the proposed incentive, participation, efficiency and financing requirements in an explicitly specified global setting. Voluntary participation must be evaluated against receiving benefits supplied by others without paying. A mechanism that makes participation attractive only by assuming that withdrawal also removes all public-good benefits would address a different problem. Likewise, a tax-backed domestic mechanism cannot establish the sovereign capability merely because it produces favorable provision or financing results.

A relevant theoretical barrier is narrower than a general claim that voluntary provision collapses in every large group. The supplied review reports that Fryxell summarizes Mailath and Postlewaite’s 1990 result for binary public-good decisions under Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality and ex-ante no-deficit, with provision costs growing at least linearly with population. In that account, provision probability tends to zero even as the probability that provision is efficient approaches one. The original paper was inaccessible in the retained artifact, so the candidate’s additional independent-private-values formulation and stronger assertion that efficiency is common knowledge remain unverified.

These distinctions matter for designing a breakthrough. A binary decision to undertake a project is not the same as choosing a continuously adjustable quantity, and ex-ante no-deficit is not the same requirement as exact budget balance in every realized outcome. Cost growth also matters: the reviewed Fryxell text reports a result attributed to Xi and Xie (2023) permitting asymptotically efficient mechanisms with an ex-ante budget surplus when provision costs grow more slowly than the square root of population. Thus, a successful mechanism must identify the assumptions under which its guarantees are possible rather than claim to overturn an unrestricted impossibility theorem.

As an engineering synthesis, practical barriers include estimating privately known benefits and costs, verifying contributions and actual provision, collecting promised payments without compulsory authority, and sustaining participation as membership and incentives change. A usable design must specify how it handles refusal, strategic misreporting, missed contributions and uncertainty about the efficient quantity. Its financing must also be explicit: external subsidies, administrative costs or recurring shortfalls cannot be omitted from a claim of budget balance.

current_state.text: The supplied review identifies Loren K. Fryxell’s Public Good Provision Re-Examined as a working paper internally dated August 22, 2024, correcting the earlier description of it as a 2026 paper. The reviewed extraction is partial and stops on page 44; the source index also records truncation. Its findings therefore support attribution to the available working-paper text, without establishing a later version, journal publication or complete examination of the document.

Fryxell proposes a cost-sharing generalized pivotal mechanism for a government with taxing authority. Its participation requirement, termed cost-sharing universal participation in the paper, differs from voluntary participation by parties who can refuse payment entirely: taxation of nonparticipants remains possible. The reviewed text contains a formal asymptotic budget-balance result under stated assumptions. An asymptotic result concerns behavior as the modeled population grows; it does not by itself establish exact financing at a particular finite scale or a practical implementation among sovereigns.

The same working paper reports that the Clarke mechanism, as defined and evaluated there, fails its cost-sharing universal participation criterion and violates asymptotic ex-post budget balance. These are useful limitations of a related mechanism within the author’s framework. They do not certify every formulation of Clarke-style mechanisms or prove that all voluntary public-good mechanisms fail. The government proposal and its reported results do not demonstrate the target capability for sovereign parties who can decline payment.

Mailath and Postlewaite’s Asymmetric Information Bargaining Problems with Many Agents is identified in the supplied research as a July 1990 article. However, the retained JSTOR content contains only an access-challenge page, so neither the proposed abstract quotation nor the theorem’s original wording could be inspected in the review. The narrower large-population account described here rests on Fryxell’s secondary discussion. The access failure limits verification; it is not evidence that the attributed result is false.

The earlier research attributes to William Nordhaus’s April 2015 Climate Clubs paper a model result that stable coalitions without sanctions on nonparticipants achieve only minimal abatement, and describes a club with trade penalties as an idealized solution. No Nordhaus artifact was supplied for the review, so those attributions could not be assessed from the available evidence. Even if verified, a coalition-model result would need to be distinguished from an implemented institution. The supplied record does not establish the current institutional status of climate clubs.

No demonstrated global mechanism satisfying the full proposed target appears in the supplied material. That is a limit of this record, rather than a finding that none exists. With no supplied freshness-search record, whether the sovereign voluntary-provision problem remains open as of November 1, 2026 is unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: sovereigns or other uncompelled parties adopt a pre-specified mechanism for one real global public good. The protocol should identify the nonpaying party’s retained benefits and establish voluntary participation relative to that outside option. A formal analysis should specify the relevant incentive concept, information assumptions and financing rule, and establish the claimed incentive compatibility, participation and budget properties. Observed compliance alone would not prove that truthful reporting or participation is strategically preferable.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: The implementation should compare participation, payments, total financing and delivered provision with pre-specified predictions and declared tolerances. Supplied quantity should reach a pre-registered, substantively large fraction of an independently estimated efficient benchmark, with uncertainty in that benchmark reported. The fraction and tolerances are proposed design choices, not established standards. Where quantity alone is an inadequate measure of efficiency, the evaluation should also examine provision costs and the benefits underlying the benchmark.
completion_criteria.label: The implementation should compare participation, payments, total financing

completion_criteria.text: Reproducibility would require an inspectable mechanism specification, proof assumptions, benchmark methods and enough implementation evidence for independent assessment. Repeated operation and tests across different participation levels, cost structures or information conditions would provide stronger evidence of reliability and scalability. Formal asymptotic guarantees should be accompanied by finite-scale bounds or measurements relevant to the actual participants. A finite collection of successes establishes demonstrated breadth within tested conditions, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducibility would require an inspectable mechanism specification, proof

completion_criteria.text: The practical boundary must remain explicit. A sanctions model without implementation, or a domestic public good financed through compulsory taxation, would not meet this proposed demonstration. If trade penalties or other inducements are included, the evaluation must explain how they affect the ability to refuse participation and what additional institutions enforce them. One successful global application could establish the capability for that setting; broader claims would require further demonstrations or applicable formal results.
completion_criteria.label: The practical boundary must remain explicit. A sanctions

related_concepts.text: ECO-09, A general, detail-free allocation compiler for private-information economies, overlaps most directly through incentive design and allocation under private information. ECO-05 has a specific institutional constraint: nonpaying parties retain public-good benefits and can refuse payment. It could be achieved through a mechanism tailored to one good without achieving ECO-09’s general, detail-free capability. Conversely, a general allocation procedure would still need to establish that its participation and financing assumptions fit this setting.

ECO-04, An interpersonally comparable, preference-respecting measure of welfare, concerns how welfare is measured across people. ECO-05 needs a defensible efficient benchmark, but could demonstrate provision relative to a declared benchmark while broader welfare-comparison questions remain unresolved. ECO-03, A predictive and welfare-coherent theory of boundedly rational choice, could improve predictions of participation and strategic behavior; it remains distinct from constructing and financing the public-good mechanism itself.

ECO-02, Prospective transport of causal policy effects across populations, is relevant when transferring a successful public-good intervention to other populations or institutions. A result in one setting does not establish that its benefits or participation incentives transport elsewhere. ECO-08, Structural counterfactuals for macroeconomic regimes, could inform comparisons of international institutional arrangements, but credible regime counterfactuals would not themselves induce voluntary contributions.

ECO-01, Empirically valid aggregate market laws beyond the Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu barrier, addresses regularities in aggregate market behavior. ECO-05 instead concerns provision and payment incentives for non-excludable benefits, although market responses could affect its costs and consequences. ECO-07, A verified, manipulable law of sustained productivity growth, could help explain benefits from knowledge provision or other growth-relevant public goods; neither a productivity law nor successful public-good financing establishes the other capability.

ECO-06, Household-scale markets for national, occupational, and housing income risk, concerns sharing private income risks, while ECO-10, Liquidity and credit without run-prone debt, concerns financial arrangements and stability. Risk-sharing or financing tools might support participants’ ability to commit resources to ECO-05, but neither resolves the incentive to receive public benefits without paying. ECO-05 remains a separate provision problem rather than a substitute for those market and financial capabilities.

change_log.change: Preserved ECO-05’s ID, title and voluntary global-public-good mechanism identity while making the benefit-retaining outside option explicit.
change_log.reason: Refusing payment while retaining spillover benefits is the central participation constraint and distinguishes this target from tax-backed provision.

change_log.change: Replaced the unrestricted large-population collapse claim with the narrower theorem account available through Fryxell.
change_log.reason: The reviewed account specifies binary decisions, Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality, ex-ante no-deficit and at least linear cost growth. The original source was inaccessible.

change_log.change: Separated efficient provision becoming highly probable from efficiency being common knowledge, and retained uncertainty about the independent-information formulation.
change_log.reason: The supplied review did not verify the stronger formulations in the candidate.

change_log.change: Added the slower-than-square-root cost-growth counterpoint and distinguished no-deficit, budget balance and asymptotic guarantees.
change_log.reason: These scientific distinctions prevent a conditional impossibility result from being presented as universal and clarify what financing claims establish.

change_log.change: Corrected Fryxell’s document date to August 22, 2024 and described its government mechanism and asymptotic budget result within their stated scope.
change_log.reason: The reviewed title block contradicts the 2026 attribution, and taxing nonparticipants changes the participation problem.

change_log.change: Scoped the reported Clarke-mechanism failures to Fryxell’s definitions and framework.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports those author-reported limitations without establishing a blanket verdict on every related mechanism.

change_log.change: Retained the Nordhaus research attribution with explicit verification and institutional-status limits.
change_log.reason: No artifact was supplied for review; missing evidence does not establish that the attributed result is false.

change_log.change: Integrated conditional impact, application-specific limits and welfare-benchmark uncertainty.
change_log.reason: Successful provision directly establishes a capability for the demonstrated setting; broader applications and particular welfare gains require additional evidence.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to include formal incentive and financing analysis, benchmark uncertainty, reproducibility and finite-scale boundaries.
change_log.reason: One observed outcome cannot establish strategic incentives, general scalability or universality.

change_log.change: Explained overlap and distinctions with every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Related capabilities can inform ECO-05 without merging their identities or making their achievement a prerequisite.

unresolved_issues: The original Mailath–Postlewaite theorem and abstract remain unverified from the supplied artifact, including the precise information assumptions and the candidate’s common-knowledge formulation.
The Nordhaus coalition result, its assumptions and the institutional status of climate clubs cannot be resolved from the supplied record because no reviewable artifact was provided.
The Fryxell extraction is partial and stops on page 44; the record does not establish a complete-document assessment, subsequent revision or journal version.
Whether a sovereign voluntary-provision mechanism satisfying the full target exists as of November 1, 2026 remains unresolved without a freshness-search record.
No specific global good, participant set, incentive solution concept, budget-balance requirement or quantitative approximation target has been selected.
Efficient-benchmark estimation, treatment of distributional values and the practical enforcement of commitments remain application-specific questions.
Any use of trade penalties or other inducements would require a precise account of whether participation remains voluntary under the proposed outside option.
